newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand extradites drug suspect to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Thailand extradites drug suspect to U.S..

text.p: Thailand on Thursday extradited under tight security a man accused of masterminding the biggest heroin haul in U.S. history.

Witnesses said about two dozen Thai police, some armed with semi-automatic rifles and sub-machineguns, provided maximum security for Li Yung Chung when he left Klong Prem prison in the northern outskirts of Bangkok.
Li, who was not seen by reporters, was said by a senior anti-narcotics police officer to be in a van that emerged slowly from the prison ringed by security men.

"Our mission is over, we have handed him over to the U.S. consular authorities. From now, we will escort him to the military airport where he will board a police helicopter that will fly him to a former U.S. airbase in Nakhon Sawan," said Police Lieutenant General Noppadol Samboonsap, head of Thailand's anti-narcotics agency.

Noppadol said a U.S. military aircraft would take Li to an undisclosed destination in the United States from the north central airbase. He would be accompanied by two U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) officers, a U.S. marshall and an embassy consular official.
He added that Li was relaxed during the transfer and had commented that he was relieved to fly to the United States because his running was over.
Li jumped bail granted by a Thai judge and fled Thailand in March but was captured and returned to Bangkok by the Burmese government last month.
A Thai prosecutor, who declined to be named, said last month that Li had spent 20 million baht ($800,000) bribing Thai officials to help him skip bail.

A Thai court subsequently approved an American request to extradite Li. Press reports said Li was concerned about his safety and feared he could be a target of assassination by those who had arranged his short escape from Thailand.
Li, an ethnic Chinese with Thai citizenship, was indicted by a New York court in May 1996 in connection with a 468-kg (1,070-lb) heroin haul in Hayward, California, in 1991.
Narcotics officials put the U.S. street value between $180,000 to $250,000 per kg, making the haul worth $87.5 million to $122 million.

Li is one of two major drugs suspects wanted in the United States who took refuge in Burma. Opium warlord Khun Sa is living in Rangoon after surrendering to Burmese troops last year in northeastern Shan state.
Burma has vowed not to extradite Khun Sa, saying the government would deal with him in its own way.
